Text | S.Li

Editing | Er Mu, Fanyu Meng

Our series on active noise cancellation (ANC) continues into 2021! Earlier articles introduced the basic principles of feedforward and feedback ANC (FF and FB ANC), and we saw that the secondary path (S(z)) is a crucial factor when computing the filter. To recap: the secondary path is the acoustic transfer function (S(z)) from the headphone loudspeaker to the error mic. See the first ANC article for how to measure it. (Note that the earlier articles used G(z) for the secondary path; this article uses S(z).)

This S(z) is highly variable. It differs from person to person (mainly because of the shape of the outer ear), and it changes with how the headphones are worn.

Figure 1. Measured secondary paths [1].

Figure 1 shows the magnitude and phase of the secondary path of the Bose QC20 (an in-ear noise-cancelling headphone) under different wearing conditions [1]. “Persons” and “dummy head” are measurements with the earphones worn normally by people and on a dummy head. Two real-world situations were also measured: 1. the earphones lying on a table (not worn, “open”); 2. the earphones’ sound outlets blocked by hand (“closed”). When the earphones lie on the table, the magnitude drops markedly at low frequencies (energy leakage). Conversely, when the sound outlets are blocked, the magnitude rises between 400 Hz and 1000 Hz. And even when the earphones are worn normally, the low-frequency response varies widely.

Normally we measure S(z) with the headphones worn normally and use it to design an adaptive or non-adaptive noise-cancelling filter. But changes in S(z) can make the filter unstable, stop an adaptive filter from converging, and so on. This article introduces methods for modeling the secondary path online, in real time.

Figure 2. Online secondary path modeling (Eriksson model) [2,3].

The first classic method uses an additional noise source to model the secondary path online [2]. The part of Figure 2 outside the red box is the block diagram of a basic FxLMS feedforward adaptive filter, where S(z) is the true secondary path and Ŝ(z) is the measured (estimated) secondary path. The part inside the red box shows how an additional noise source is used to measure the secondary path in real time. The secondary path estimate is updated iteratively with the LMS algorithm, and the result is used in the feedforward FxLMS noise control system. So the diagram contains two adaptive systems: one cancels the noise, the other models the secondary path. Let’s look at how 𝐒̂(n) is updated (inside the red box):

𝐒̂(n+1)=𝐒̂(n)+μs𝐯(n)f(n) (1)

Here n is the discrete time index, μs is the step size, and 𝐯(n) is the noise produced by the internal noise generator. Bold symbols denote vectors. Now let’s see what the modeling error f(n) is made up of:

f(n)=e(n)−v′̂(n)=d(n)−(y′(n)−v′(n))−v′̂(n)=d(n)−𝐬(n)*𝐲(n)+𝐬(n)*𝐯(n)−𝐬̂(n)*𝐯(n)=𝐬(n)*𝐯(n)−𝐬̂(n)*𝐯(n)+d(n)−𝐬(n)*𝐲(n) …(2)

Because the system runs two adaptive systems at once, and both use the same error mic as their error sensor, the update of 𝐒̂(n) converges only if v(n) and 𝐲(n) are uncorrelated; otherwise the LMS adaptive system will struggle to converge. Even then, the two adaptive systems interfere with each other, because part of each one’s error signal always belongs to the other. For the secondary path adaptive system, x(n) is the disturbance; for the FF ANC adaptive system, the internal noise v(n) is the disturbance.

Building on the Eriksson model, Zhang proposed an improved structure that reduces this mutual interference [4] (Figure 3), improving the convergence of both the noise control and the secondary path modeling systems. How does it work? By introducing yet another adaptive system (H(z), in the green box) whose sole job is to remove the part where the two interfere with each other.

Figure 3. Online secondary path modeling (Zhang model) [3,4].

As you can see, unlike in the Eriksson model, the residual noise measured by the error mic is not fed directly to the FF ANC adaptive filter. Instead, the disturbance term v′̂(n) introduced by the secondary path adaptive system is removed first. Likewise, the residual noise measured by the error mic is not fed directly to the secondary path adaptive filter; the disturbance term z(n) introduced by the FF ANC adaptive system is removed first.

Figure 4. Real-time weighting of secondary paths [5].

Guldenschuh proposed a fairly practical way of keeping the ANC adaptive system from failing to converge when the secondary path changes [5]. The principle is simple. First, the secondary path is measured in two situations: worn normally (Ŝ1), and with heavy leakage, for example when the headphones cover only part of the ear or are lying on a table (Ŝ2). The two secondary paths are weighted and summed for use in the ANC FxLMS computation. Inside the system, an 18 Hz infrasonic signal is generated to detect how the headphones are being worn. As Figure 1 showed, when there is leakage, the low-frequency magnitude of the secondary path is smaller than when the headphones are worn normally. A correlation measurement can therefore determine the current wearing condition and, from it, the weights of the two secondary paths. Since infrasound is, in principle, inaudible, the method does not affect the noise cancellation.

There are, of course, many other methods for modeling the secondary path online, but most of them have not left the lab, and they still have some way to go before they reach real products.

About the author: S.Li

An acoustics PhD student who has been roaming Germany for years, working mainly on binaural audio, psychoacoustics and active noise control.

References

[1] S. Liebich, J. Fabry, P. Jax and P. Vary, Acoustic path database for ANC in-ear headphone development, ICA, 2019.

[2] L.J. Eriksson and M.C. Allie: Use of random noise for on-line transducer modeling in an adaptive attenuation system. J. Acoust. Soc. Am., 85(2) (1989), 797–802.

[3] Y. Kajikawa, W.-S. Gan, and S. M. Kuo. “Recent advances on active noise control: open issues and innovative applications.” APSIPA Transactions on Signal and Information Processing 1 (2012).

[4] M. Zhang, H. Lan, W. Ser: Cross-updated active noise control system with on-line secondary path modeling. IEEE Trans. Speech Audio Process., 9(5) (2001), 598–602.

[5] M. Guldenschuh. “Secondary-path models in adaptive-noise-control headphones.” 3rd International Conference on Systems and Control. IEEE, 2013.
